video_title: A Goldman M&A Banker Helped Bring the Olympics to Los Angeles | Odd Lots
gist: Live from the Future Proof conference, Odd Lots interviews Gene Sykes — Goldman Sachs partner, chair of the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee, IOC member and head of the original Los Angeles Olympic bid — who lays out the LA 2028 economics (no new construction, athletes housed at UCLA, 15 million tickets, NBC rights through 2036) before pivoting to his day job: he says this is the biggest M&A year on record, driven by AI and the infrastructure build-out beneath it. He argues only ~2% of companies have so far reported an actual EPS benefit from AI even though 20-30% have implemented strategies, that this AI build-out is funded by cash-rich hyperscalers rather than the venture capitalists who financed the 2000-01 telecom bubble, and that AI should make back catalogs more valuable, not less.

insights.claim: The Los Angeles 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games are being staged with no government funding for the event itself, with the federal government's role limited to security and security-related logistics for the 206 countries sending teams.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Tests whether the 'privately funded games' template is repeatable; if LA28 avoids the public cost overruns that plagued prior hosts, it changes the municipal-credit and bid-economics calculus for future host cities.
insights.quote: it's essentially privately funded in that there's no government support to put the games on, with the exception of the federal government playing a role in security and security related logistics

insights.claim: Los Angeles plans to build no new venues and no athletes' village for 2028, housing all athletes in existing UCLA residences that already accommodate more students in a normal year than the Games will require.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Removes the capital-expenditure and white-elephant-infrastructure risk that has historically sunk host-city budgets, meaning construction and real-estate plays tied to past Olympics largely do not exist in this cycle.
insights.quote: We have more stadia and arenas and world class places where sports already takes place. So we don't have to build anything.

insights.claim: Roughly half of LA 2028 tickets have already been sold, everything offered in the first release sold immediately, and the next ticket release is not until the following year — with prices set deliberately at market because ticket revenue must actually fund the Games.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Strong early sell-through is the clearest live indicator that the private-funding model will clear its revenue targets and that U.S. inbound-event demand has not been damaged by the political environment.
insights.quote: They are priced at the market and it's going to take a lot of ticket sales to actually pay for these games.

insights.claim: Olympic traffic congestion is treated as a solvable information problem rather than a capacity problem: LA's 1984 experience showed that pre-announcing disruptions changes driver behavior, and existing HOV lanes will be converted into dedicated Olympic lanes.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Operational risk that historically generates negative pre-Games press appears low here, reducing the reputational tail risk sponsors are underwriting.
insights.quote: People behave based on what they know and what they're expecting to happen.

themes.theme: Olympic Scale vs. World Cup Benchmark

insights.claim: The combined Olympic and Paralympic Games in Los Angeles will involve roughly 17,000 athletes, about 900 medal events and 15 million tickets sold, versus a World Cup with 104 matches across 16 stadiums, roughly 600 athletes and 6.5 million tickets.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Quantifies the Olympics as roughly 2.3x the World Cup in ticket volume with vastly more governing bodies and stakeholders — a useful sizing anchor for hospitality, travel, advertising and logistics exposure into 2028.
insights.quote: in the Olympic and Paralympic Games, when you put the two together, we'll have 17,000 athletes

insights.claim: The Olympics is the one major sports property whose audience skews female rather than male, a fact the speaker says most people do not realize.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Explains why consumer brands like Coca-Cola, Visa, Starbucks and Samsung pay premium sponsorship rates for the Olympics specifically — it reaches a demographic other sports inventory cannot.
insights.quote: the Olympics are the one sports experience that skews toward women more than toward men

insights.claim: The 2026 World Cup was a net reputational positive for the United States as a host, with visiting fans finding America welcoming and the event materially changing how American audiences relate to soccer, despite mixed global perceptions of American politicians.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Supports the view that inbound international-event tourism to the U.S. is not being materially suppressed by the political climate — relevant to airline, hotel and hospitality demand forecasts into 2028.

themes.theme: Olympic Media Rights and Clean-Venue Sponsorship

insights.claim: NBC holds U.S. Olympic media rights through 2036 under a deal worth roughly $1.5 billion or more per Games, committing to host cities that have not even been selected yet.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Locks in a decade-plus of contracted Olympic revenue visibility for the IOC and a fixed, non-negotiable content cost line for NBC/Comcast through 2036 regardless of how linear TV economics evolve.
insights.quote: it's, you know, a billion and a half dollars or more per games to, uh, to have the rights in the United States

insights.claim: Olympic sponsorship is sold in two tiers — the IOC sells global rights to firms like Coca-Cola, Visa and Samsung, while the local organizing committee separately sells domestic rights, with LA28 already signing Starbucks, Uber and Google.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Names the specific corporates taking on LA28 marketing spend; the dual-tier structure means domestic sponsorship is incremental revenue the host committee controls and is central to the private-funding math.

insights.claim: The Olympics enforces a 'clean venue' rule prohibiting any corporate advertising in the field of play, deliberately forgoing the in-venue ad inventory that FIFA monetizes heavily, and LA28 has no plans to relax it.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Caps a revenue line competitors exploit, which means Olympic monetization must come from rights fees, sponsorship and tickets — and preserves the scarcity/premium of the brand that sponsors are paying for.
insights.quote: If you've been in Olympic Games and you see the field of play, you'll notice there's no corporate advertising anywhere in the field of play.

themes.theme: Record M&A Cycle and Its Closing Window

insights.claim: This is the biggest M&A year in history by a wide margin, expected to exceed the prior 2021 peak that was inflated by Covid-era conditions, and the activity is described as deep rather than concentrated.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: A record advisory-fee pool supports investment-bank earnings; the comparison to 2021 also flags that the prior peak was followed by a sharp drought, so the cycle position matters for bank revenue durability.

insights.claim: Sales of private-equity-sponsor-owned companies have accounted for about 40% of the M&A market in recent years but are running closer to 30% this year, because strategic, technology-driven demand has grown faster than sponsor exits.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Shows the record M&A year is being driven by corporate strategics, not sponsor exit backlogs — a healthier, more thesis-driven mix, though it also means PE dry powder and exit queues are still not clearing proportionally.

insights.claim: Corporate boards are currently biased pro-deal out of a fear-of-missing-the-window mentality — a belief that transactions impossible five years ago are now achievable and that the opening is temporary.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: This is the classic late-cycle tell: a deal window driven by urgency rather than fundamentals typically closes when financing tightens or regulators turn, so expect deal announcements to front-load and then fall off sharply.
insights.quote: There's a sense that now the world is open to this kind of transaction, and if you don't do it, you're you're probably going to lose the opportunity.

insights.claim: The 'merger of equals' structure is a cosmetic device: split boards and shared management teams exist to get deals signed at a premium, but within about a year of closing, decision-making power consolidates into one set of hands.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Investors should underwrite announced mergers of equals as acquisitions — governance concessions are transient, so integration risk and the eventual winner's culture, not the announced power-sharing, determine the outcome.
insights.quote: the influence to make decisions for the company tends to consolidate into a set of hands

insights.claim: Roughly 80% of startups are built with a sale to another company as the intended endgame, and only the 20% with something genuinely differentiated ever become sustainable independent companies.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Reframes venture portfolios as M&A supply rather than IPO supply, implying the exit environment for most private AI companies depends on strategic acquirer appetite, not public-market receptivity.
insights.quote: for 80% of the startups, the end game is selling themselves to somebody else

insights.claim: SpaceX became an enduring independent company because it differentiated by defying the regulatory environment that incumbent competitors accepted as fixed, rather than by out-executing them within it.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Suggests a screen for identifying the rare startups that will not be acquired: those whose moat comes from a regulatory posture incumbents cannot adopt.
insights.quote: the incumbents played in a regulatory environment that SpaceX decided to defy

insights.claim: Anthropic and OpenAI are expected to remain independent because they have already grown too large for anyone to acquire, making their durability a bet on the platform rather than on an exit.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Removes the acquisition backstop from valuations of the largest AI labs — late-stage private investors are underwriting standalone platform durability or an eventual IPO, with no strategic floor beneath them.
insights.quote: They're almost too big for anybody to buy.

insights.claim: A boom in semiconductor equities and semiconductor M&A is being driven by companies across every industry wanting to own proprietary semiconductor technology rather than buy it.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Implies a persistent strategic bid under semiconductor IP and design assets from non-traditional acquirers, which supports valuations for smaller chip-design targets.

themes.theme: AI Build-Out vs. the Dot-Com Precedent

insights.claim: The key structural difference between the current AI infrastructure build-out and the 2000-2001 telecom/internet build-out is who is funding it: cash-generative mega-cap technology platforms now, versus venture capitalists then.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: The funding source determines how a bust transmits — equity-funded capex by cash-rich incumbents impairs earnings rather than triggering the credit and bankruptcy cascade that followed the fiber build-out.
insights.quote: the investors in this build out are the most successful big technology platforms anywhere in the world who had hundreds of billions of dollars of free cash flow until this year

insights.claim: The phrasing that hyperscalers 'had hundreds of billions of dollars of free cash flow until this year' concedes that AI capex is now consuming the very cash cushion that supposedly makes this build-out safer than the dot-com one.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Watch hyperscaler free cash flow, not capex guidance, as the stress indicator — if the self-funding argument erodes, the build-out shifts to debt and the dot-com analogy gets stronger, not weaker.

insights.claim: Whether the AI infrastructure being committed today is oversized relative to demand five or six years out is genuinely unknowable, and a senior Goldman dealmaker declines to claim otherwise.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: The absence of conviction from someone with full deal-flow visibility is itself signal: nobody underwriting these deals has a demand model they trust, so position sizing should reflect genuine uncertainty rather than consensus confidence.
insights.quote: are we, uh, committing to build too much infrastructure relative to the real demand that we're going to see 5 or 6 years from now? I think the answer is we just don't know.

insights.claim: Only about 2% of companies have stated in earnings reports that AI usage has produced a positive impact on EPS, while roughly 20-30% have actually implemented AI strategies across their operations — a measured gap between deployment and demonstrated financial return.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: The single hardest number in the episode: at 2% EPS attribution, the AI productivity thesis embedded in equity valuations is almost entirely unrealized, and that ratio rising (or not) over coming earnings seasons is the cleanest scoreboard to track.
insights.quote: 2% are the companies who, in their earnings reports have said we see an impact on EPs, a positive impact of our use of AI.

insights.claim: Giving employees a ChatGPT or Claude subscription amounts to glorified search and does not constitute meaningful enterprise AI adoption, which would mean AI deeply embedded in the workflow.
insights.speaker: host (Joe Weisenthal)
insights.so_what: Suggests headline 'AI adoption' survey figures and seat counts overstate real penetration; the investable signal is workflow integration and reported EPS impact, not subscription attach rates.
insights.quote: That's a glorified search

insights.claim: At Goldman Sachs, the youngest employees are effectively AI-native and are implementing applications the firm was not contemplating a year earlier, delivering more capacity per person and shifting the type of problems staff work on.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Internal adoption led from the bottom of the seniority pyramid implies headcount leverage rather than headcount cuts near-term — watch revenue-per-employee at the banks as the first place AI shows up in financials.

insights.claim: AI will not make M&A advisers smarter but will give them more and better information faster, raising confidence and judgment quality — and will reset what clients expect from advisers even though dealmaking remains a trusted-relationship business.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Frames AI in advisory as margin-expanding rather than disintermediating, which favors incumbent franchises with relationships over AI-native challengers in high-touch financial services.
insights.quote: it's not that they're becoming smarter, it's that they have access to more information, better information, and that allows him to have more confidence and better judgment

themes.theme: AI, Media IP and Back Catalogs

insights.claim: AI is expected to make existing content libraries and back catalogs MORE valuable, not less, because it will discover more uses for already-seasoned content — extending a decade-long trend in which catalog cash flows have been securitized.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Directly opposes the commoditization thesis; supports continued bid for music and film catalog assets and the ABS structures built on their royalty streams.
insights.quote: I think AI is likely to make existing contents in catalogs more valuable because it will find more uses for existing content

insights.claim: Reaction to AI within media splits by self-confidence rather than by sector: music-industry incumbents are anxious and focused on defending against misuse of licensed content, while creators treat AI as a tool that lets them produce work beyond their own technical competence.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Predicts the fight over AI in media resolves through licensing and rights enforcement rather than outright displacement — favoring rights-holders who can strike licensing deals over pure-play catalog defenders.

insights.claim: TikTok's recommendation algorithm, built in China over a decade ago, is cited as the only product ever created by a Chinese company that the rest of the world genuinely wants to buy, and as a precursor to modern AI personalization.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: A senior dealmaker treating algorithmic recommendation as China's one globally exportable product frames the strategic value of the TikTok algorithm in any ownership or divestiture negotiation.
insights.quote: the only Chinese person, or only Chinese company, to have created something that the rest of the world really wants to buy

insights.claim: Voice-cloning and AI-replication services for personalities are already being pitched commercially, with the speaker confirming that agents are actively encouraging creators to try such out-of-comfort-zone, high-upside offerings.
insights.speaker: Gene Sykes
insights.so_what: Signals that likeness and voice licensing is moving from speculation to an actual transaction market, creating a new monetizable asset class for IP holders and a new rights-clearance liability for media companies.
